utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-02-60-T, the Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. This is a hearing in accordance with Rule 50(A)(i)(c), which says: "The Prosecutor may amend an indictment, (c), after the assignment of the case to a Trial Chamber, with the leave of that Trial Chamber or a Judge of that Trial Chamber, after having heard the parties." Following the Krstic appeal's judgement, the Prosecution filed a motion for leave to file fourth amended joint indictment on the 14th May 2004, and the Defence filed his response on the 26th May 2004. On June the 3rd, 2004, the Prosecution filed a reply to the Defence response. I believe that the position of both parties on this issue are clear; however, in order to facilitate the discussion of this proceeding at first I would like to invite both parties to summarise their views very briefly. After that, the Judges might ask some questions to both parties, concerning of the issues raised in their motions. We understand that the parties might hold different views on this issue. The purpose of this hearing is for the parties to present their representative positions, respective positions, sorry, but not to invite the parties to engage in heated debate on legal issues. Well, having said that, could I turn to the Prosecutor. Yes, Mr. Shin, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Mr. President, members of the Trial Chamber. Your Honours, the Prosecution relies, basically, on its written submissions, and in accordance with the President's wishes seeks here merely to provide a brief overview of its arguments, firstly; secondly, to focus, provide a little more focus on the specific legal issues that the Trial Chamber has previously indicated interest in, and specifically that would be the relationship between aiding and abetting in genocide, and complicity in genocide; and thirdly, the Prosecution will just comment briefly on -- or rather, raise some additional comments to some of the arguments raised by the Defence in their response brief. And of course, the Prosecution will be prepared to respond to any questions from Your Honours and perhaps as well to respond to any additional points raised by the Defence. The Prosecution submits that the motion to amend the indictment should be granted for the following reasons: First, an amendment to the indictment is permitted within the discretion of the Trial Chamber under Rule 50 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence and under the jurisprudence of this Tribunal. The Defence, as we understand it, does not dispute that. The issue is really whether there's any prejudice that would be occasioned upon the accused by accepting the proposed amendments to the indictment, and the Prosecution would submit there is no prejudice here, because the material facts that underlie a charge of aiding and abetting in genocide -- and I'll slow down, thank you, Mr. President. Underlying accounts of aiding and abetting in genocide, those material facts were already set out in the currently existing indictment and further detailed in the Prosecution's pre-trial brief. On the first point regarding the Prosecution's right to seek an amendment to an indictment, I won't make any further comment other than to briefly refer to a recent decision in the Limaj case dating from the 12th of February, 2004, in which leave to amend the indictment was granted. We would just note that that decision observed that new charges have been added in cases before the ICTY and the ICTR, even in the absence of new factual or evidentiary material. We would also just note, and this is in paragraph 8 of that decision, we would also note that that decision generally held that: "A decision to accept an amendment would normally be forthcoming unless prejudice can be shown." On the issue of prejudice, the Prosecution submits, in short, that there is no prejudice to the accused here resulting from the proposed amendments to the indictment. We turn first to the Krstic Appeals Chamber's decision from, I believe, the 19th of April, this year. The Krstic Appeals Chamber's judgement found that aiding and abetting genocide established where the accused in that case, A, had knowledge of the genocidal intent of others; and, B, made a substantial contribution to, again in that case, the execution of Bosnian Muslim prisoners, and I refer here to paragraph 137 of that judgement. The Prosecution submits that the material facts that would support a charge of aiding and abetting genocide is articulated, as that charge is articulated by the Krstic Appeals Chamber's judgement, have already been detailed in the current existing indictment. In short, the accused has already been put on notice by the existing indictment for criminal conduct that constitutes aiding and abetting genocide. And the Prosecution would point to, for example, the facts pleaded in paragraphs 35 to 54 of the indictment. And I won't go -- unless Your Honours would like, I won't go any further into these specific factual allegations. The Prosecution would submit further that notice of -- notice to the accused that he was being charged with criminal conduct that we see now constitutes aiding and abetting genocide was also provided to the accused in the Prosecution's pre-trial brief and again here. I'll just cite briefly to -- among other sections of the pre-trial brief, paragraphs 100 to 111. And the summary of those factual allegations, as set out in paragraph 113. In further support of the Prosecution's argument that the accused has already been put on notice and therefore suffers no prejudice by a charge of aiding and abetting genocide, the Prosecution would point to its discussion of the legal elements of complicity in genocide, set out both in the indictment, paragraph 54, and also in the pre-trial brief, paragraph 206 and 207. In the indictment, the Prosecution alleged that, A, the accused was an accomplice in the commission of a crime; B, the crime was committed; and C, the accused knew of the genocidal intent of those who perpetrated that crime, and therefore the Prosecution was charging the accused with complicity in genocide. Now, the Prosecution would submit in this regard and in this additional argument and support of the Prosecution's position that the accused has been put on notice, the Krstic Appeals Chamber judgement in fact provides further assistance. What the Krstic Appeals Chamber judgement has done, we would submit, is definitively clarified that there is an overlap between conduct that constitutes aiding and abetting genocide under Article 7(1) and Article 4(3)(a), and that covered by complicity in genocide under Article 4(3)(e) of the Statute. We would submit that this overlap is clear on the face of the judgement. If we look at paragraph 139 of that judgement, for example, we see express reference to the consequent overlap between Article 7(1) and Article 4(3)(e), and the Appeals Chamber said that that consequent overlap was not inadvertent. It explains a little later in that paragraph that it was not inadvertent because in that case, or rather, to quote it completely: "In this case the two provisions can be reconciled because the terms 'complicity' and 'accomplice' may encompass conduct broader than that of aiding and abetting." We would submit that this shows clearly the position of the Appeals Chamber that complicity in genocide encompasses conduct criminalised by a count of aiding and abetting in genocide. Now, the Prosecution recognises also that the Krstic Appeals Chamber judgement goes further and indicates that complicity in genocide not only encompasses the conduct criminalised by aiding and abetting in genocide, but may also include conduct beyond that. Now, we would submit that the full scope of the conduct that would constitute complicity in genocide is not set out in the Krstic Appeals Chamber judgement, and that is for the simple reason that it was not necessarily for them to fully articulated the contours of the complicity in genocide in order to find in that case that Mr. Krstic was guilty of aiding and abetting in genocide. What we would say, though, and reiterate, is that it is clear that there is this overlap of complicity in genocide and aiding and abetting in genocide. There may be, as we see in paragraph 139 in that provision that I just quoted, that conduct constituting complicity in genocide may go beyond that that goes beyond conduct that constitutes aiding and abetting in genocide. But we do note that the Appeals Chamber makes some caveats in making -- in providing that discussion. For example, in footnote 247, the Appeals Chamber expressly states that they are not seeking to make a finding as to the appropriate mens rea for complicity in genocide. So in short, we would say that the Appeals Chamber decision in the Krstic case makes it clear that when an accused has been charged with complicity in genocide he should also have been put on notice of conduct that's criminalised under aiding and abetting in genocide. The Prosecution would reiterate here, as it has set out in its written submissions, that it is fully prepared to proceed on the indictment as it stands if our motion is denied. And that's for the simple reason, again, that the Krstic Appeals Chamber judgement makes it clear that, first, complicity in genocide remains a viable charge, and secondly, in light of the reasoning of the Krstic Appeals Chamber judgement, we would submit that complicity in genocide fully encompasses the count of aiding and abetting, or rather, conduct that's criminalised by aiding and abetting, and of course complicity in genocide is a count in our existing indictment. However, the Prosecution will note that it did not intend in its currently existing indictment to charge the accused with a crime that entails the genocidal intent on his part. Our intent had been to charge him with criminal conduct that entails the knowledge of the genocidal intent of others. The Krstic Appeals Chamber judgement suggests now that the charge of complicity in genocide may go beyond conduct that constitutes aiding and abetting genocide and they stray in the conduct that entails the specific intent for genocide. And I will refer to, in particular, the first sentence in paragraph 142 of the Krstic Appeals Chamber judgement in that regard where, and I quote, the Appeals Chamber states: "By contrast there is authority to suggest that complicity in genocide, where it prohibits conduct broader than aiding and abetting requires proof that the accomplice had the specific intent to destroy a protected group." In conclusion, the Prosecution submits that the motion to amend the indictment should be granted because the proposed amendment would bring the indictment in line with this recent jurisprudence from the Appeals Chamber and accord more fully with the original intent of the Prosecution in charging Mr. Blagojevic. Secondly, the proposed indictment is otherwise permitted within the discretion of the Trial Chamber, by Rule 50 and Tribunal jurisprudence, where there is no prejudice to the accused. And we would submit that here there is no prejudice to the accused. The material facts supporting a charge of aiding and abetting in genocide have already been fully pleaded under the heading -- under the count of complicity in genocide in the indictment and also in the pre-trial brief. Just a quick word on Rule 50(B) and (C), we have submitted that, in our written submissions, that Rule 50(B) and (C) should not apply here because we submit essentially what we have here is a recharacterisation, a legal characterisation of an existing charge, and not, we would submit, a new charge within the meaning of Rule 50. We do recognise, however, that the Trial Chamber may take a different view, that a plea under Rule 50(B) would be necessary. But we would reiterate here that the real issue, the core issue, is whether there is prejudice to the accused. We submit that there is none but even were the Trial Chamber to apply Rule 50(B) and (C) in this instance, we would reiterate that there should be -- there is no rationale or basis in this context for any delay in the continuation of the trial. Finally, I'll just turn briefly to a couple of the arguments raised by the Defence in their response brief. First, the Defence seek to make much of the timing of this motion to amend the indictment and the Prosecution's motivation or reasoning behind it. We would submit that those -- these issues are, first of all, adequately addressed in our written submissions. And secondly, that they distract from the core issue, which is whether there is prejudice to the accused in this instance. On the point of timing, I think we've made it clear that we filed our motion as a response to the Krstic Appeals Chamber judgement. If that Appeals Chamber judgement had come earlier, we would have filed our motion to amend the indictment earlier. Secondly, the accused seeks also to make much of the fact that in prior amendments, the Prosecution dropped the genocide count against Mr. Blagojevic and maintained only the complicity in genocide count. Again, we believe this has been addressed in our written submissions, but we would just note that at the time the existing indictment was addressed to Mr. Blagojevic, it was the position of the Prosecution that conduct that we now see under the Krstic Appeals Chamber judgement should be characterised as aiding and abetting in genocide. The Prosecution has the position that that should be articulated as complicity in genocide. And in particular, the Prosecution was seeking to charge Mr. Blagojevic with a crime that entailed the knowledge of the genocidal intent of others and not with having genocidal intent himself. So that's -- that, we believe is clear, is -- explains why it is that we had at one point dropped the genocide charge and maintained the complicity in genocide charge. At this point, in light of the Krstic Appeals Chamber judgement, we believe it would be in most keeping with the developing jurisprudence to amend this to aiding and abetting. Finally, we would just reiterate that the core issue here is whether there is prejudice to the accused for the reasons we've previously set out in our written submissions, and here today there is no prejudice to the accused arising from this amendment, from the proposed amendments. The Defence does allege that they have suffered prejudice, but they do so in a conclusory fashion, and fail to articulate exactly how it is that prejudice has arisen. We would submit, in short, following the Krstic Appeals Chamber judgement, there can be no prejudice. Complicity in genocide, as set out there, encompasses aiding and abetting in genocide. So a charge of complicity in genocide in the indictment has fully put the accused on notice of the conduct that constitutes aiding and abetting in genocide. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Shin. Now, I turn to the Defence. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. I will apologise in advance for not having as eloquent and as polished as I should be for this sort of a momentous occasion, in light of the ongoing activities with the trial and the late filing of the reply by the Prosecution, which we received on Saturday, for whatever reason. In any event, let me just begin by saying if they thought all along that Mr. Blagojevic was only guilty of aiding and abetting, what pray tell stop them in charging him simply with aiding and abetting? What? Was it Madam Del Ponte telling them, no, proceed with higher charges? What stopped them? If you look at their pleadings, their initial pleadings, they tell us why they are seeking this indictment to be amended. And they say specifically: "The Appeals Chamber addressed the relation between complicity in genocide under Article 4(3)(e) on the one hand, and aiding and abetting in genocide on Article 4(3)(a) and Article 7(1)." That's what they initially state and that's on paragraph 2. And incidentally, when I look at the Krstic judgement, it doesn't say anything about 4(3)(a). It just says 4(3). But those are their stated reasons, nothing about what they say later on after they filed their reply, without seeking leave as they should have, but nonetheless they state here on paragraph 10: "The accused appears to have fundamentally misunderstood the essence of the Prosecution's position as set out in the motion. In short the Prosecution submits that the Krstic Appeals decision has, from its perspective, expanded the count of complicity in genocide beyond the charge the Prosecution intended. The Prosecution did not intend to charge the accused, Blagojevic, with a crime entailing genocidal intent, but rather, with knowledge of the genocidal intent of others." So finally, after all these years, the Prosecution now says: This is all we wanted to charge him with. My question is: Why didn't they just simply have a charge aiding and abetting in genocide? They could have done that simply at the very beginning. But if you look at the history of this case, initially, they charge him with genocide, and in the alternative, complicity in genocide. For whatever reason, they decided to drop the genocide. Curiously, curiously, and this has puzzled me, to be honest, when Nikolic was charged, even after the indictment was amended, he was charged both with genocide and complicity in genocide, which I thought was oxymoronic, because how can you also have the command responsibility and have a lower-ranking officer charged with a higher crime? It never made sense to me, but I never questioned them. But it would seem to me that they had made some calculated decisions. Now, I've read the Stakic decision, which is quoted in Krstic, and I've done some fairly deep thinking on what the Prosecution has been trying to do all these years and I've finally figured it out. All along they have been trying to promote the idea that in genocide with respect to complicity, you don't need the special intent. That has been the modus operandi from the beginning of this institution. Because by lowering the bar you can get a charge, you can get a conviction on genocide, even though the founders and the drafters of the genocide convention never intended that. That's my opinion from my reading of the history of the convention, that when you look at and when you specifically look at 4(3) and all the different modes, it's clear that you need intent. Now, let's look -- let's leave genocide aside for a second. With respect to aiding and abetting, there has been jurisprudence in this Tribunal. In other modes of liability, or other crimes I should say, where it's clearly stated that for aiding and abetting you only need knowledge, knowledge of the intent of others. So if somebody's about to kill someone and they say: "Can I borrow your gun to kill," and you say: "Go ahead," you're aiding and abetting because you know the intent of the person. So to say today, finally, finally, we've figured it out that for aiding and abetting we only need knowledge, and not intent, and now we have some certainty because of Krstic, I find it, to be honest, rather intellectually disingenuous. And what I really think, what I really think is Krstic, the Krstic Appeals' decision does not give us so much certainty with respect to the legal articulation of genocide and complicity - but I'm going to get to that - but rather, when they see the factual findings in Krstic, and knowing that this case, and the Krstic case, factually are almost identical, which the exception that in this case they have far less evidence than in Krstic, then it becomes crystal clear that there's no way on earth that they'll be able to meet the burden of proof, that is, that of genocidal intent, which is required for complicity. And so, they're reading the tea leaves in the Krstic decision. That's what my submission is and that's what the timing is. Now, let's look at the Krstic judgement, the appeal judgement. And I dare say that I have some problems with this judgement, some major problems. I also understand that under the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, that the Trial Chambers have to apply the law from the Appeals Chambers, something that I learned in this case with respect -- on other issues. So I'm intimately familiar with that, on the application of Appeals Chamber decisions at the trial level. But when you look at the Krstic judgement, and I dare say, history will not be kind to this judgement, unfortunately, it will not. First and foremost, I have problems with the fact that they make reference to Stakic, not because I don't like the Stakic judgement, in fact, I'm mootful in that sense and I know we have two distinguished members of the Stakic panel from the trial level. And in fact, there is one part that I definitely like, and I'm going to talk about that. But what I find troubling, what I find most troubling as a jurist or as a lawyer, that here is a case that's on appeal, in other words it's being appealed to the second Chamber; it is not finalised; and the Appeals Chamber - which eventually is going to have to make a decision on that case - is now using that to bootstrap its argument in the current appeal. In other words, by doing so, how can the Stakic lawyers then turn around and mount an appeal against the very same body that has accepted the Trial Chamber's decision in order to fashion and form an argument or a decision to another appeal argument? Very difficult. Furthermore, and I say this with the utmost respect for this institution, though I have some problems in the way its organised, is the fact that you have the Presiding Judge of Stakic also sitting on the Krstic judgement, the appeal judgement. And I'm not saying there was any impropriety, but I am saying that there is the appearance of impropriety, or at least the appearance of partiality. How can the Presiding Judge of the Stakic decision Trial Chamber then sit on the Appeals Chamber and at the same time making reference to the Stakic decision in order to say: Now we have established law? And I think if you look at the footnotes - and I do this with the utmost respect for the members of the Appeals Chamber, but if I were on the Bench with them I would have had some disagreements with them - but when you look at their footnote 231 and 232, they refer to Stakic as if Stakic is law. Stakic is on appeal. They're going to be hearing that case. So I think before we rush to judgement about how good the Krstic appeal judgement is in this case, I think we need to pause. And as I said, history may not be kind, but it will take another Appeals Chamber to find cogent reasons. Perhaps they will listen to part of my argument and find those cogent reasons, at least in part in overturning some portions of this decision. But going further into the Krstic decision, and I hope I'm not too bombastic for this fine institution, but I do get emotional; I can't help it. That's part of my personality. But I do get emotional when I see such things as saying -- for instance, they go on to say about the many domestic jurisdictions both in common and civil law, with respect to the mens rea when it comes to aiding and abetting and what have you. When you look at it, they cite France, Germany, Switzerland and England. Then you see a citation to the United States. We know from the United States that very few states, and not in the federal system, do they say that you accept that or aiding and abetting you do not need intent. You also need the intent; it's not just mere knowledge. So there seems to be a problem. But you have only, rather than many jurisdictions, you have four jurisdictions here with respect to aiding and abetting and genocide, and I think that's very important. Perhaps that's where the Prosecution may have an argument like, well, you know, we didn't think that you could have -- there was no law with respect to aiding and abetting in genocide, that you only needed knowledge. That's where we went astray. But as I said earlier, their intended purpose from day one was to lower the bar so they could get a conviction of the crime of all crimes. Curiously enough in the Krstic decision, as was pointed out by the Prosecution, they ducked the very same issue that they had to discuss in my opinion, which was complicity in genocide. They didn't discuss it at all. What reasons? I don't know. They do speak about the overlap between 7(3) and 7(1), and I want to speak about that a little bit. It was touched on in the Stakic case, both at the 98 bis judgement and in their decision. And what I liked about the Stakic case is the fact that they said, the lex specialis and the lex generalis, I liked that part. In fact, I think that's what this those folks had in mind, unless, of course, you buy into the Appeals Chamber's discussion and say, "oh, no, there was no inadvertence, there was no overlap. And therefore 7(1) applies to the Articles from 2 to 5." The problem with that is, when you get to Article 4, which is genocide, it's taken right off the convention, it also has the different modes of liability. You know, you can be genocide, conspiracy in genocide, complicity, incitement, all of that good stuff. So they already included all of that, because I think and I believe that the drafters always had in mind that if you're going to be convicted for genocide, you have to have that special intent. And I dare say, and maybe this is my own personal position but even for aiding and abetting. But as far as applying 7(1) to 4, to Article 4, you have to apply it all the way down the list. Because they don't make any differentiation here in the Krstic judgement. So therefore, if we extend their argument-- let's take aiding and abetting and conspiracy to commit genocide. What's a conspiracy? Joining an organisation to commit a crime, right? Well, how can you possibly just aid and abet conspirators? Once you begin to assist in a conspiracy have you not joined the conspiracy? Are you in and out at the same time? Can you just aid the conspiracy without becoming a co-conspirator? It doesn't make much sense. Then if we go to our particular case and if we apply the logic I just heard then it would seem to me there's no need to amend the indictment because the Trial Chamber could very easily find that there is such a thing as aiding and abetting complicity in genocide. Why not? If you look carefully at the judgement of the Appeals Chamber, it doesn't make the distinction, it doesn't say that it's directly to 4(3)(a), which is genocide. At least that's how I've read it. I've read it over and over again. Perhaps I'm too tired and too old to figure it all out, but that's how I see it. It doesn't make sense. The Prosecution says, you know, we never intended to charge anything but knowledge, but if you deny us this motion we're prepared to go forward on a charge which we know is not supported by the evidence and we never intended. So it puts us between a rock and a hard place. Of course, how could a Defence lawyer stand up here and say, wait a second, why wouldn't you want to lower the charges of your client. What I'm saying and what they're trying to do is lower the bar of what they have to prove, because now they realise, midstream, that what they've been saying all along, that we have a man here who had genocidal intent, now they're saying, "We need something and better to get something with genocide on it than nothing." I dare say that's what happened in Krstic. Because also what I find difficult to swallow in Krstic is the fact that the Trial Chamber -- the Appeals Chamber on its own reached down and made that determination as to aiding and abetting. It was never argued by the Prosecutors, it was never pled. It was never argued by the Defence. It was never much of an issue. Krstic had been convicted of genocide. So if he's not convicted of genocide, then you go to complicity in genocide. So for complicity in genocide, we need the special intent. Here the Appeals Chamber says, we're not going to deal with that issue. We're just going to go further down the ladder, and so the question is: Can they do that? Well, in my opinion, the way I see it, here is my interpretation of it, if we were in the common law system, I think the answer would be no. Why? Because the accused would have a right to have a choice whether he wanted a lesser included offence to be considered by the finder of fact. That's how it is. So even though you have a lesser included, the accused may decide, no, I want to roll the dice. What you charge me with, I don't want any of the lesser included to be considered. There was a very famous case a couple of years ago, it was a nanny case in the United States, which was rather significant. They chose, the Defence lawyers for whatever reason chose not to go with manslaughter, and then afterwards, the jury found for the higher offence, and then they went back to the judge and asked the judge to overturn the jury's verdict on the basis that it did not meet the evidence. In the continental system, or the common-law system, I think we're in a rather different system, because they have a different legal tradition. I'm not a specialist but I think I understand it well enough, and in that system, I think and I believe, that the judges have a different function and the Judges can go, no doubt in my mind, the judges can, on their own, say thank you, Mr. Prosecutor, but you missed the boat on that one. There is something, you haven't charged it. But it has to be within the indictment. I think in Germany it may be slightly different, the judges may be allowed to go outside the judgement, or the indictment, I mean, in order to look for evidence, but by and large I think in the continental system the judges can look into the indictment, even if it's not specifically pled in the indictment, if it's a lesser included, the judges on their own have the power to reach down and say, the facts meet this particular crime. And I'm sure you'll correct me if I'm wrong on that. Now, we come to this Tribunal, we have a hybrid system, a little bit of both. My position has always been rather consistent. In court, we have an adversarial system. Very much so. But the legal tradition is, I think, for all intents and purposes, very continental in mind. Why? Because, I think in these sorts of crimes the judges have a special responsibility to make sure the victims are not re-victimised because the Prosecution has failed to properly charge the accused, and at the same time to protect the accused in the event they have some sleeping lawyer who is not protecting them. So I think I will have to agree with the Prosecution that in this particular case the Court does have the right to exercise its discretion, even at this stage to amend the indictment, if it sees it's necessary. We don't have any additional facts in this case, so we are not prejudiced from that standpoint, in other words they're bringing in new charges. We don't have that. You know, we're very clear on that. Had we been prejudiced -- I think we've been prejudiced already. I think Mr. Blagojevic perhaps might have had a shot to be provisionally released, he wasn't, because they made him out to have this genocidal intent. So we have been prejudiced, whether we would have tried the case differently, or prepared the case differently, I can assure you yes. Well, the Prosecution can say, tell us how. It's not for me to tell them exactly how I would have challenged the indictment to start with, how I would have mounted a defence, because I mounted a defence based on challenging intent, knowing that if I can get past that hurdle, then maybe we may get tagged with a lower hurdle but at least I've overcome the big one. If the bar is lower, then of course I'm shooting at the lower bar. And you can't say, it's all-inclusive. It may sound that way, but it isn't that way. Plus, You also have to take into consideration that we have limited resources. So you would target your resources differently. Can I say concretely I would do this and that differently? No. Can I say concretely and exactly how I'm prejudiced? No. We prepared a case based on the indictment, and I think as it was stated in Kupreskic, it says here, the Appeals Chamber emphasised: "The Prosecution is expected to know its case before it goes to trial." Well, they should have known their case, and I certainly knew my case and my case was based on their case. Now they're telling me, for the first time I learn on Saturday, all along I had it wrong. All along, all they intended to charge him with is a crime he had knowledge and not intent. And I submit, Your Honours, the reason they state that is because all along they have been promoting this concept that complicity in genocide only requires knowledge and not intent. They have been trying to shove this down the throat of the Tribunal. And over and over again, they have been told no. And I think it's not amount of clarity. They knew it from the get-go that they needed intent, but they were trying to push this concept to lower the bar because it's easier to get convictions. I think the drafters of the genocide convention saw genocide as the crime of all crimes. And I think the Krstic decision dilutes it. Now, what you do, I think, is up to you. I believe we have been prejudiced. I believe that I will have to switch gears at this point in time. I think it's sort of late in the game. The timing of it, of course, they say, well, Krstic just came out. Of course, yeah, Krstic just came out and they got slapped in the face. They said, you know, the facts that you have weren't good enough. You can't prove intent. Not to mention, and I failed to mention this, another point I find rather curious about Krstic, they're saying he aided and abetted, he had knowledge in assisting some folks that had genocidal intent without saying who they were. How could he know who they are or what their intent was, this special intent, if the Trial Chamber didn't identify them? I just think that this Appeals Chamber decision is rather weak on the law and on the reasoning. I think it's expansive. I think it dilutes the concept of genocide. I don't think it gives us much clarity. I think it will be overturned in some fashion when cogent reasons are articulated in another case. And I don't think the Trial Chamber in this particular case has to apply this decision because it's not directly in this case. The Prosecution is raising it; they made the motion. We leave it up to the Trial Chamber to make its decision whether they should amend the indictment or not. I think you have the right. I think that's where we agree with the Prosecutor, that you have the power, even at this point in time, to amend the indictment. We believe we've shown some prejudice. Can I show more? Concretely, no. But then again, I should not be in a position where I have to disclose my trial strategy and how I would redo it all again on a hypothetical. They're trying to get into the sanctum sanctorum of the Defence. I think that's a bit too much. I don't know if I was very helpful, Your Honours. I apologise for not being as polished as I would have like to have been, and perhaps I wasn't as clear or as thoughtful, but I hope that I was somewhat helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Stojanovic, are you going to join this discussion?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Your Honour, I wish to raise a few points from the viewpoint of our Defence. You have seen from the fourth amended indictment that there is not a single word modifying the earlier indictment regarding our client, Mr. Dragan Jokic. Practically, this entire discussion has turned into a debate concerning the modification of the indictment with respect to the accused Blagojevic, and if we understood it correctly, for the purpose of charging him now with aiding and abetting in light of the recent Krstic Appeals judgement, rather than complicity in genocide. Since not a single word of modification has been suggested in respect of our client, either in terms of legal qualification or description, the question arises: Are we able at all to object to this motion to amend the indictment? Because we seem to have exhausted our right to object concerning the third amendment of the indictment. I believe we have no grounds for objecting, because there are no new facts and no new charges that would prejudice our client. Instead, a different debate has been opened here and we observed in it that there is no supporting practice in this Tribunal. According to the judgement under 98 bis, we received the decision handed down by this Trial Chamber which stipulates that after the completed Prosecution case our client has not been proven to be individually responsible on counts 2 to 5, whereas he is responsible, liable, for all charges under counts 2 to 5, as a person who has aided and abetted this crime. You know that after the legal proceedings that took place here, as to whether this decision should have been sought to be revoked by interlocutory appeal or otherwise, the decision of our Defence team was not to proceed with an appeal. In the legal system where I come from, such a decision is legally valid and effective. Excuse me, Your Honour, I was just informed that the record states that we did not appeal. What I meant to say was that the Prosecution did not appeal and after the expiry of the given deadline, the decision became effective. In this sense what is at issue here is the res judicata. For our Defence team, the decision is effective in the part which concerns aiding and abetting. In the specific situation, our Defence team believes that the -- had the Prosecution had persisted in its previous qualification rather than abiding by the decision of the Trial Chamber, in the belief that it will be able to adduce additional evidence after the Defence case and succeed in proving the individual responsibility of our client. It remains for us to adduce evidence in our Defence case, to prove that he is not liable, even on the charges of aiding and abetting. What we wish to emphasise today while subscribing to everything that the Defence counsel of Mr. Blagojevic said, is that there can be no aiding and abetting without intent, without premeditation. Mere knowledge of the existence of a crime, that is the crime itself and its perpetrator, cannot be the only reason underlying somebody's criminal liability. In addition to knowledge, intent is required as well. It remains to be seen whether it is intent to perpetrate, be an accomplice in, or aid and abet. And that is the question of how we value and judge the evidence. In light of the experience of this Tribunal, individual responsibility indubitably requires intent on top of knowledge. In other words, it is necessary to prove that our client had the intention to aid and abet the perpetrators. In conclusion, we would like to join in the arguments presented by the Defence of Mr. Blagojevic and to reiterate the theory which seems purely academic to us, because the indictment does not charge Dragan Jokic with any mode of liability and genocide, and that was finally clarified under the decision of 98 bis. Somebody cannot be properly convicted of complicity or aiding and abetting where the perpetrators are not specified. From the Krstic appeals judgement, it seems to transpire that genocide was committed by members of the Main Staff. The judgement does not say who the perpetrators were, but still the judgement does make a step further and says that somebody, in this case Krstic, aided and abetted the unidentified perpetrator. This is a highly unusual situation in which time and jurisprudence will have the final word. However, as far as our Defence team is concerned, this is an academic discussion, because as I mentioned the amended indictment does not charge us with any mode of liability under genocide. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. It is very helpful for the Bench to know your position on this issue and your position is registered in the transcript. Yes, Mr. Shin, I give you less than five minutes for a very concise reply, if there's any.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I don't think I'll even need the full five minutes. First, I would just point out that the Defence for Mr. Jokic did not file any motions on this issue, and we would submit that they, in fact, have no standing to make oral submissions on this point. We acknowledge that they state -- this is an academic discussion and we take that to be acknowledgment on their part that they do not have standing to make oral submissions here. Just to note also for the Defence for Mr. Jokic, I'm not sure if I misunderstood this in the transcript, but the 98 bis decision as we read it does not include the word "committing" in its judgement of acquittal -- in respect of Mr. Dragan Jokic. So that may have been an error in our understanding. As regards the Defence submissions for Mr. Blagojevic, we heard a lot about speculations on the motive of the Prosecution, the structure of the Tribunal, and other issues relating to Article 4, other than what is at issue here. On the issue that is relevant here on prejudice, the Defence has essentially admitted that there is some prejudice but not much. And we would submit that some prejudice is merely a conclusory reiteration of this claim of prejudice without any substance behind it. And finally, we would just note that the Prosecution intends to keep its concerns about the Krstic Appeals Chamber decision to ourselves. But in any case, the Krstic Appeals Chamber judgement is the law. We are a tribunal of law and we are bound by that decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe that the Judges may have some questions to both parties. I think first of all we would like to address a question to the Prosecution. Well, as the Prosecution claimed if the criminal conduct that the Prosecution is charging Mr. Blagojevic with is already included in complicity in genocide, as submitted in the motion, why did the Prosecution request leave to amend the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, in brief, the Krstic Appeals Chamber judgement indicates that complicity in genocide, which we had previously considered to be essentially the same as aiding and abetting in genocide, does indeed overlap with aiding and abetting in genocide but also goes further than that and may entail conduct, may criminalise conduct, that also entails the specific intent for genocide. As it was clear in our indictment, and I refer specifically to paragraph 54, the intent of the Prosecution was to charge the accused with criminal conduct with the knowledge of the specific intent of others. To the extent that this extends -- that the results of the Krstic Appeals Chamber judgement is that the charge, as it stands now, extends beyond that, we think it would be appropriate to make this amendment. In addition, we also note that the Appeals Chamber judgement in Krstic found that under facts which, as the Defence themselves have indicated are very similar to the facts of this case, that aiding and abetting in genocide would be the proper characterisation of the criminal conduct in that case. Now, I think one issue that may have -- that may be behind some of the submissions of -- made today by the Defence is that there is in some respect, perhaps, something that's counter-intuitive about the concept. Complicity in genocide may entail genocidal intent, and aiding and abetting in genocide may entail a mens rea of knowledge of the specific genocidal intent of others, but in any case that is the jurisprudence coming out of the Krstic Appeals Chamber judgement. And in light of that, we thought it would be appropriate and believe still that it would be appropriate to file the amendments to the indictment, as set forth in the motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Vassylenko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: If the amendment of the indictment is not granted by this Chamber, is the Prosecution indicating that the Trial Chamber should not go beyond that part of complicity in genocide which reflects aiding and abetting?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that is the Prosecution's submission, and indeed, to reiterate, that's why the Prosecution does believe that the amendment would be appropriate, in order to circumscribe the criminal conduct that's being alleged to what the Prosecution had intended by its language. And we're not speaking about now some other motive or intent of the Prosecution, other than as reflected in the language of the existing indictment. We believe that the amendment would bring the charge in line with what was intended. And just to add also, that as the -- as the Krstic Appeals Chamber judgement indicates, if complicity in genocide is to include both conduct -- criminal conduct coupled with knowledge of the genocidal intent of others and potentially also - and I emphasise potentially there, because of course that's a dicta from the Appeals Chamber judgement on that issue - but also to include criminal conduct coupled with the genocidal intent, I mean, in short our position is that it would be preferable to focus -- to bring the indictment in line with the more specific charge, specific to what the Prosecution intended in charging Mr. Blagojevic with complicity in genocide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Argibay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: This is perhaps a technical question, but do you find a difference between Article 4(3)(e) and Article 4(3)(a) behind this proposal of amending the indictment? I mean, would you -- a finding of aiding and abetting genocide more properly be reflected under Article 4(3)(e) than 4(3)(a)?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, in light of the Krstic Appeals Chamber judgement, which we must work with in this regard, we believe that as that judgement found or as the Appeals Chamber found in that case, that aiding and abetting in genocide would be the more proper characterisation of the count -- of the charge. And certainly in line with the specific language in the indictment that the Prosecution had sought to charge Mr. Blagojevic with. I'm not sure if that answers your question, but I'm happy to expand further, if it would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Do you have -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Do you think that there is a hierarchial relationship between Article 4(3)(a) and Article 4(3)(e)?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would hesitate, for the purposes of this motion, to set out a position beyond the specific teaching of the Krstic Appeals Chamber judgement on this issue of aiding and abetting in genocide and complicity in genocide. So I don't think in that context it would be appropriate for us to take a view as to the hierarchy of the elements within Article 4, except to say that what is relevant from the Krstic Appeals Chamber judgement here is what they have said about complicity in genocide, that it encompasses aiding and abetting in genocide and may go further. And that's what has occasioned us to file the instant motion to amend the indictment. And that's where we believe that the amendment would bring it more in line with the jurisprudence from the Krstic Appeals Chamber judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: One more, only one more. You have submitted that the amended would reduce the liability of Mr. Blagojevic under Article 7(1) of the statute. But what impact, if any, could the amendment have on his alleged responsibility under 7(3)?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Well, to be frank, Your Honour, we haven't addressed that specific issue. I think our view is that that's not specifically an issue for the purposes of this amendment, for the amendment that we're seeking at this juncture. But we don't believe that there should be any impact on Article 7(3) in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, there are some questions addressed to the Defence. I'm not sure that I understand -- fully understand the Defence's position, especially on the issue of whether the complicity in genocide is a form of liability for the crime of genocide. If so, how could we define this form of liability, or does the Defence understand the complicity in genocide to be a distinct act or distinct crime?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you for asking that question, Your Honour, because I believe it ties in with the second-to-last question by Judge Argibay and I would like to address both of them. Well, the Prosecution, first of all, in paragraph 9 of their initial motion says, and I quote: "The Krstic Appeals Chamber judgement affirmed that complicity in genocide is distinct from aiding and abetting in genocide, and in that sense there can be no question that the legal characterisation of count 1(B) of the indictment is viable on its face." If I understand the Prosecution's position, and my reading of the Krstic is: You have genocide and then you have complicity or conspiracy and what have you. Under genocide, perhaps as a lesser included, you would have aiding and abetting, because that's how I see it at least, with complicity being somewhat different, which is why in order for them -- if you buy into their argument, in order for you to find aiding and abetting, they have to re-charge under genocide. So in other words had they allowed -- had they kept the indictment as it was initially, they would still have the possibility of you finding aiding and abetting because genocide is there as a lesser -- so aiding and abetting would be the lesser included in genocide. Not having genocide, then you come to this dilemma, as was pointed out earlier, which is: Well, can you have aiding and abetting in complicity in genocide? So does 7(1) apply to 4(3)(e)? It's almost, for lack of a better term, you know legally absurd to go that route. But if you look at the Krstic judgement, it's very unclear, because it just says we look at 7(1) and 7(1) was poorly drafted -- that's what my opinion is, as opposed to the drafters had something else in mind, I think it's poor draftsmanship, and in retrospect nobody picked up on it and here we are. 7(1) is not a problem for Article 2, it's not a problem for Article 3 and it's not a problem for Article 5. It becomes a problem for Article 4 because you have 4(3), (a), (b), (c), (d), (e). That's where the problem arises. And I think if you read the Krstic decision, they -- and I've read it several times. I believe what they're saying is complicity in genocide is separate from genocide, and therefore, they don't even touch complicity, they don't deal with it, but rather, they say the facts in this case go to knowledge and therefore that would be a lesser included in the genocide. And I think that's why the Prosecutor panicked, because when they looked at their indictment and say, my God, we took out genocide, now how do we get there? Which brings you back to the question, Judge Argibay, that you asked which is: Well - or Judge Vassylenko, I don't know which one of you, but one of you - what if you go to trial -- what if you proceed, are you saying that we should only find aiding and abetting in complicity? Since you're telling us now, the cat is out of the bag, as it were, that all you wanted from day one was aiding and abetting, all you're saying is he had knowledge. If you keep it and don't change the indictment, aren't you telling us that we could only find aiding and abetting in complicity in genocide? You see. That's what's happening over here. And of course we on the Defence side do have some concerns with 7(3). I didn't address them, but I think there's some -- there's an article by Mr. Schabas, a renowned expert on genocide. He talked about that, especially with respect to the Krstic judgement. But frankly I've been a little overwhelmed in the last few days with other matters and I didn't pay much attention to 7(3), otherwise I would have mounted a defence on that. But I do think there are some implications between you're talking about command responsibility and the imputed intent or knowledge of the commander. So there are some implications. And with all due respect to my colleagues on the other side, they haven't defended the case, they haven't put a defence. It's easier to construct a Prosecution than to mount a defence. It's a different methodology, a different approach; so we are prejudiced. But I don't know if I'm answering your question, Mr. President. I see them as distinct. I see aiding and abetting as part of genocide. Perhaps that's why if the statute is ever amended, 7(1) should say, included in Articles 2, 3, 4(3)(a) so it excludes all the others. Because as I indicated, can you be an aider and abettor to a conspiracy to commit genocide? Have you not joined the conspiracy by aiding the conspiracy? At least in the United States, which is sort of the flavour of the day of every Prosecutor in the federal system, because it's a big net, conspiracy, the moment you do anything with respect to the co-conspirators, you become a co-conspirator. So that's aiding and abetting. So how can you become an aider and abettor in a conspiracy? It means you're in the conspiracy and at the same time you're out. It's, as I said, rather legally absurd. And that's why I think, and I probably agree with the Prosecution, though they don't want to take a position on this one, it's kind of disturbing because they're hedging for other cases I would suspect, but they should come clean and just tell us, you know, that they're distinct. And that's why they want to amend the indictment. And all I'm trying to do, Your Honour, is get the truth out. What are we really here about? They want to focus me on the issue and I want to focus on the facts. Because I believe the motivation behind the Prosecution is they're seeing that they cannot get a conviction that has genocide on it unless somehow, this Trial Chamber --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object at this point to this argumentative -- going into his case now; arguing genocide; wrapping in U.S. conspiracy law into this discussion, which has nothing to do with joint criminal enterprise law, nothing to do with this discussion; it's highly prejudicial; it has nothing to do with the issues that are addressed. So I will just say at this point I think it's enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, I think I understand your position on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I got carried away, Your Honour. I apologise. But I don't think it's prejudicial to anybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You did not specifically say how would the amendment affect the preparation required by the Defence. Of course, you -- I believe that you have no obligation to disclose your case, your strategy, but we need a little more detailed information. I hope you could furnish this information as far as you could. Of course, we do not force you to lay your cards on the table.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well -- very well, Your Honour. There are few cards, as there are in any defence, but we'll play them well. First of all, first and foremost, as you well know, the first thing that a lawyer does is challenge the indictment. And So based on how the indictment would have been prepared, we would have mounted a different motion practice with respect to that particular indictment. Secondly, there is the different interplay between 7(1) and 7(3), and you know with -- we always went along with the understanding that since he's charged with complicity in genocide that I had to mount a defence that included special intent. And so in packaging our defence, we always kept that in mind. Now, the Prosecution says: Well, there is this overlap. And I'm willing to concede that there is a certain amount of overlap, because I do believe -- and perhaps in answering Judge Argibay's question is that if it's a lesser included, you look at it as a pyramid. I've always -- that's how I teach it is that, you know, you start with knowledge and then if you go up the ladder, if you had intent you would have had knowledge plus intent, because you can't have knowledge -- intent without knowledge. So you go up the ladder. So if you're looking at a -- say for instance, in a murder case you would have negligence, then recklessness, then knowledge, then intent. And That's how you get all the way to the top. So if you look at it that way, as a pyramid, you would have knowledge as a stepping-stone before you get to genocide. When you get to complicity, it's a little bit different and -- but I have to concede and I'm willing to concede that in preparing this case, of course I'm always preparing with the understanding that knowledge is a stepping-stone. But again, I have to emphasise that with the limited resources that we have, I'm going to mount a different defence if all I have to do is attack knowledge versus attacking intent. That's -- so that's -- I think a prejudice that's hard to put a handle on at this point in time because I'm two weeks away from resting. And at this point in time, I have to confess, it's very difficult for me to stop and smell the roses and try to figure out, how would I do this all over again? I'm just trying to keep my nose above the water. So there's that. And I haven't -- I know that there is a significant interplay between 7(1) and 7(3), particularly 7(3) and Article 4. And of course we would have -- in my opinion, we would have investigated the case differently, perhaps brought different witnesses here, more witnesses dealing with knowledge versus the intent. The Prosecution has claimed on many occasions that Blagojevic was in meetings. Being in a meeting, that would denote that he was part of the planning process versus maybe hearing about it. So as I -- I believe that we have been prejudiced, and I think that we will be prejudiced. On the other hand, I will concede that the Trial Chamber has to apply the law, and the question is: Now that that's being brought to the Court's attention by the Prosecutor they don't have the evidence or they never had the intent. Why they never expressed it earlier, I don't know. I'm a little upset, but I guess I should be glad. But they never really mentioned it before that all they wanted was knowledge, not intent. But now they've come clean. So the question is: What do we do? I leave that up to you, Your Honours, because I'm in a difficult position, as you could understand. If I were in my own legal tradition, I would be playing it a little differently. But here, I understand that the Judges can act on their own in order to make sure that justice is done at the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, at this stage are there any matters that -- yes, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could just in one minute respond to some of the issues raised there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Counsel for the Defence has made references to "cat out of the bag," "coming clean." If we just turn to paragraph 54 of the existing indictment it says very clearly: "The conduct of - Mr. Blagojevic - met the requisite three elements of complicity in genocide." The third one there is: "The accused knew that the crime was being committed" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I was speaking too quickly there. I'll slow down. I'll re-read that paragraph. "The conduct of Vidoje Blagojevic met the requisite three elements of Complicity in Genocide, namely that" -- and I'll go to C -- "The accused knew that the crime was being committed in furtherance of the intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnic, racial, or religious group, as such." So frankly, we don't understand where -- what the Defence is getting at about this sudden revelation. This is in the existing indictment. That's all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just a matter from yesterday, if we could go into private session. It's nothing very extensive, but something I've discussed briefly with Mr. Karnavas that I would like to discuss with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So we are leaving this subject?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah -- well, when you are finished with it, of course. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go to private session, please. Well, it seems to me that we have some problems with the communication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I guess that we have exhausted this topic, and the Bench will withdraw for the deliberation of the ruling concerning of the request filed by the Prosecution. The hearing is adjourned , and we'll meet at 2.15 in the courtroom this afternoon.
